signals.summary: Patrisia Macías-Rojas excavates the failed precursor bills behind AEDPA and IIRIRA, showing how proposals that tested unchecked executive power over immigration 'lay in waiting' before consolidating into law — a history-of-ideas argument that defeated legislation still shapes the state.

signals.title: Fascism's Building Blocks: A US Infrastructure Decades in the Making
signals.summary: A. Naomi Paik and Catherine S. Ramírez introduce a series arguing that today's 'unprecedented' emergent fascism is in fact precedented — built on the 1986 IRCA and the three 1996 statutes (AEDPA, IIRIRA, PRWORA) — revising the liberal narrative of Trumpism as rupture into one of decades-long bipartisan infrastructure.

signals.title: Magic by Return of Post: How Mail Order Delivered the Occult
signals.summary: Allan Johnson argues that the turn-of-the-century American occult revival was an infrastructure story: Linotype machines, cheap pulp paper, and improved postal networks made mail-order magic possible, revising the picture of occultism as anti-modern mysticism into a product of industrial modernity.

signals.title: Twilight of the Velocipede: Typesetting Races before the Age of Linotype
signals.summary: Alex Wright recovers the lost world of competitive hand-typesetting races — thousand-strong crowds, big cash prizes — and shows how women compositors ('Swifts') used them to fight for workplace equity, reframing the pre-Linotype print shop as an arena of labor politics rather than a doomed craft awaiting automation.

signals.title: Animal, Vegetable, Lamb: The Zoophyte from Tartary
signals.summary: Thom Sliwowski traces the medieval legend of the Vegetable Lamb of Tartary — a half-plant, half-animal hybrid — reading it as Europe's garbled apprehension of cotton and of distant commodity frontiers, a micro-history of how premodern knowledge systems metabolized the unfamiliar.

signals.title: The Continued Revival of Mahjong: The Indonesian Youth Edition
signals.summary: Screen-fatigued Indonesian millennials and Gen Z are packing mahjong lounges in Jakarta and Surabaya — Four Winds' founder was converted by the Crazy Rich Asians mahjong scene, while Riichi Indonesia spreads the Japanese variant as a competitive 'mind sport' through national festivals and world championships. The revival is layered with Chinese-Indonesian memory: the game was effectively restricted under Suharto's 1967 Presidential Instruction, so its café-culture return doubles as heritage reclamation and analog social repair.

signals.title: From East to Eats: Indonesia's Martabak Manis Crosses Borders
signals.summary: Viewpoints essay tracing how martabak manis, once the sugar-dusted secret of Jakarta street vendors, has become a global sensation reworked with matcha and modern toppings — an argument about how a humble pancake carries generational legacy and Indonesian identity as it travels, part of RADII's June theme of culinary storytelling as a map of identity and migration.

signals.title: All Aboard the Love Train at China's Metro Station Marriage Markets
signals.summary: Matchmaking corners are migrating from parent-run park marriage markets into metro stations in Hefei, Guiyang, Nanjing, and Suzhou — Hefei's Xinghua Park Station logged over 4,000 QR-code sign-ups and Xingfuba Station's in-metro marriage registry has wed 5,600 couples since 2024, including 200 on May 20 ('520') this year. Young professionals prefer these self-authored, commute-integrated profiles to the parental-pressure version, advertising hobbies and personality instead of height and hukou.

signals.title: From Labubu to Beyblade: Asian Adults Are Playing Again
signals.summary: Across Southeast Asia, 'kidult' culture — Labubu queues, Pokémon card nights, Beyblade tournaments, Gunpla builds — has expanded from blind-box collecting into a lifestyle and social identity, read here as a coping mechanism for a generation whose traditional adulthood milestones feel financially inaccessible. Chinese brands like POP MART and MINISO normalized adult toy spending via immersive lifestyle retail, while Xiaohongshu turned collections into signifiers of cultural awareness.

signals.title: Vinyl Bars, Film Cameras, and the Rise of Asia's Analog Revival
signals.summary: From Bangkok listening bars to Seoul vinyl cafés and Kuala Lumpur film-camera communities, Gen Z and millennials who never grew up with analog media are driving a region-wide turn to tactile rituals and slower consumption as resistance to digital overstimulation. The piece notes Asia's distinct flavor: unlike Western music purism, the revival here fuses with lifestyle design, emotional consumption, and café culture — and was ironically amplified by Xiaohongshu and Instagram aestheticization.

signals.title: Meet 021: The Creator Community Redefining Art Beyond Commerce
signals.summary: Profile of 021 ('zero to one', Shanghai's city code), a creator community founded by Sydney Jingzhi Hu that occupied the club OASIS in March and took over Beijing's X Museum in May with ambient-music series ELSEWHERE, funk nights, art runs ending in raves, and AI-audio workshops. Framed by the founder's question 'If society is a factory, then what is art?', it exemplifies China's third-space movement testing how creativity can grow alongside, not under, commerce.

signals.title: Barmacy: Gen Zs Are Getting Healthy While Getting Drunk
signals.summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine bars like Niang Qing — herbal cocktails, in-bar pulse readings, full-body diagnoses — are sweeping Chinese cities as the latest evolution of 'punk wellness', the ironic health regime of a generation that calls itself cuipi ('crispy/fragile'). The contradiction is the point: knowingly wrecking yourself while performing self-repair turns burnout into shared community humor.

signals.title: Is China Falling Out of Love With Its 5A Tourist Attractions?
signals.summary: As the official 5A scenic-site list balloons to 358 entries with almost none ever removed, Chinese travelers are revolting against hidden shuttle-bus fees (Changbai Mountain's 105 RMB ticket becomes 270 RMB with mandatory buses) and drifting toward Citywalk, Colorwalk, and 'reverse travel' to obscure destinations. The piece argues authenticity and chill now outrank official rankings — bloggers have even coined a nonexistent '6A' tier for places that still feel special.

signals.title: Communiqué 113: Masobe Books' bet on digital subscriptions to save Nigeria's reading culture
signals.summary: As inflation reshapes reading habits in Nigeria, publisher Masobe Books is betting its ebook subscription app can succeed where OkadaBooks failed — an analysis of whether digital pricing can keep literary consumption alive in a squeezed economy.

signals.title: Communiqué 114: How Tech Safari turned one newsletter into a group of businesses
signals.summary: A case study of Tech Safari's evolution from a single newsletter into a multi-vertical media group with a six-figure recruitment arm, a diaspora fellowship, and an events business — a template for how African niche media monetizes community rather than ads.

signals.title: Communiqué 115: The economics of a microdrama
signals.summary: Africa's microdrama economy is forming on sub-$20,000 production budgets, importing the vertical short-drama format from China and adapting its unit economics to local screens — a new low-cost video grammar reshaping what gets watched and funded.

signals.title: Communiqué 116: The product thinking creator
signals.summary: Africa's creators have mastered audience-building, but converting that audience into a durable business is a different and largely untaught skill; the essay argues creators must adopt product thinking — designing offerings, pricing, and retention — rather than chasing reach alone.

signals.title: Communiqué 117: The creator-athlete era comes to Nigeria
signals.summary: From the Carter Efe vs Portable celebrity boxing match to Kings League-style formats, creator-athletes are building a new sports-entertainment economy; the essay maps what this hybrid of influence and athletics could mean for Nigeria's sports business.

signals.title: Communiqué 118: The clipping middlemen driving attention in the creator economy
signals.summary: In Nigeria, 'clipping' — middlemen who cut and redistribute creator content across platforms — has become the de facto distribution engine of the creator economy, but unresolved tensions over payment and consent expose the cracks in an informal attention market.

signals.title: Communiqué 119: Africa's missing tech industry canon
signals.summary: Africa's tech industry has produced billion-dollar companies but almost no authoritative books or long-form accounts of how they were built; the essay argues this missing canon weakens institutional memory and lets outsiders define the industry's story.

signals.title: Communiqué 120: The gospel of narrative non-fiction, according to Eghosa Imasuen
signals.summary: Through publisher Eghosa Imasuen, an examination of what it takes to build a canon of African narrative non-fiction — the editorial, commercial, and cultural infrastructure required for the continent to document itself rather than be documented.

signals.title: Have you considered publishing fewer stories?
signals.summary: A media-business essay making the case for 'The Great Slowdown' over 'The Endless Scroll' — that publishers drowning audiences in volume should publish less, better, as the smarter economic and editorial strategy.

signals.title: Make dress codes clear again.
signals.summary: Uses a billionaire investor's request for 'sexy party clothes' at his Brooklyn party as a jumping-off point to argue for explicit dress codes, reading the anxiety around ambiguous ones as a status-legibility problem in elite social life.

signals.title: Nothing too late, nothing mistake.
signals.summary: Argues that the future of media looks like Kareem Rahma and his friends — personality-led, low-overhead franchises built outside legacy institutions — and examines what their model means for traditional publishers.

signals.title: Holy water.
signals.summary: A look into Loonen, the bottled water favored by the coastal elite — how a commodity product gets turned into a class signifier and what its rise says about status consumption in 2026.

signals.title: How did David Protein's ice cream get on Bella Hadid's yacht?
signals.summary: Unpacks celebrity product seeding by tracing how David Protein's ice cream ended up in Bella Hadid's yacht content ('She is a fan,' the company insists), a case study in how engineered brand moments are made to look organic.

signals.title: What happens if you go through the Surf Lodge portal?
signals.summary: On how Montauk's Surf Lodge has become a full-body sponsorship billboard — this season fronted by nicotine-pouch money — and what the venue's transformation reveals about the brand-activation economics of Hamptons nightlife.

signals.title: All you need is a phone, WiFi, and a little creativity to make money on OnlyFans.
signals.summary: An examination of the low-barrier economics of OnlyFans creator work — the platform's pitch that a phone, WiFi, and creativity are enough to earn — and what that promise looks like in practice for the people chasing it.

signals.title: Vogue taps more Substack writers.
signals.summary: Emily Sundberg gets Vogue editor Chloe Malle to explain the magazine's strategy of recruiting Substack writers, an analysis of legacy fashion media absorbing independent newsletter talent rather than competing with it.

signals.title: I got stood up by an AI agent, and tracked down its human owner in China
signals.summary: Viola Zhou tracks down a Chinese solo entrepreneur who pays a quarter of his salary to let AI agents run his side-hustle app — and who discovered his artificial 'employees' have been keeping secrets from him. A vivid, on-the-ground portrait of the one-person AI company as an emerging mode of work and self-conception in China's hustle economy.

signals.title: How the vinyl revival fills the gaps streaming left behind
signals.summary: Indranil Ghosh examines the global vinyl resurgence and finds that the reasons people buy records diverge sharply across cultures — what reads as analog nostalgia in one market functions as archival preservation, status display, or resistance to streaming's homogenized catalog in another. A reminder that the same 'retro' consumption trend carries different identity work in different places.

signals.title: The Chinese whiz kids of Silicon Valley
signals.summary: Viola Zhou's feature traces how Chinese-born tech workers, long the quiet engine of Silicon Valley, have become superstars in the AI era — examining the identity bind of researchers celebrated for their talent while caught between U.S.-China rivalry, surveillance suspicion, and competing national claims on their loyalty and genius.

signals.title: The Filipino virtual assistants behind LinkedIn's 'thought leadership' content mill
signals.summary: Michael Beltran reveals that Filipino virtual assistants earning around $7 an hour use AI tools to ghostwrite LinkedIn posts and comments on behalf of Western executives — the polished 'personal brand' of the Western professional class is literally manufactured in the Global South, exposing the outsourced labor beneath the aesthetics of authenticity.

signals.title: China's tech rise is creating a new kind of tourism
signals.summary: Kinling Lo reports on foreign visitors flocking to China's factories, AI startups, and tech campuses in search of the next breakthrough — an inversion of the old grand-tour logic in which the West was the destination for glimpsing the future. Tech tourism to Shenzhen and Hangzhou is becoming a consumption category and a status experience in its own right.

signals.title: Pope's encyclical raises questions on who gets to shape AI
signals.summary: Rina Chandran argues that the papal encyclical on AI, while offering an ethical and moral framework, is steeped in Catholic doctrine and ignores the faiths and practices of the majority of the world's population — making it a case study in how even 'universal' AI ethics is being written from a particular cultural seat, and what it means for non-Western religious worldviews to be absent from the conversation.

signals.title: Silicon Valley's lure is fading for India's tech talent
signals.summary: Ananya Bhattacharya reports that India's elite engineers are starting to see U.S. big tech jobs in a new light — the Silicon Valley posting is losing its status-symbol power as domestic opportunities, visa hostility, and a recalibrated sense of where the future is being built shift aspiration back home. A marker of how the geography of professional prestige is being rewritten outside the West.

signals.title: Big Tech, big cons: Scammers are hiding in the apps that make your life easy
signals.summary: In an excerpt from her book 'Bharat Bluff: Inside the Cons of India's Internet Revolution,' Soumya Gupta shows how fraudsters exploit the trust newly online Indians place in Google, Facebook, and WhatsApp — the everyday platforms of India's internet revolution have become the very infrastructure of its cons. A portrait of how digital trust, a core consumer good of the platform era, is being weaponized in the Global South.

signals.title: Why (Wellness) Marketers Use the Same Tactics as Cults with Dr. Mara Einstein
signals.summary: Marketing scholar Mara Einstein details how cult recruitment techniques structure the wellness and diet industries, with Weight Watchers and MLMs as case studies — community, identity, and escalating commitment doing the selling that product efficacy can't.

signals.title: Leaky Gut Syndrome: Real Condition or Dubious Diagnosis?
signals.summary: Harrison tells the story of a woman who came to attribute all her health issues to 'leaky gut,' then untangles the actual science of intestinal permeability from the catch-all alternative-medicine diagnosis — part of her running 'dubious diagnoses' series on how vague labels capture patients.

signals.title: Why Beauty Imperatives Are Not Victimless Crimes ft. Elise Hu
signals.summary: Interview with journalist Elise Hu (Flawless) drawing on her modeling and disordered-eating history to argue beauty culture is a 'cousin' of diet culture — the same body-optimization imperatives migrating from weight to skin and face, with real costs rather than victimless self-improvement.

signals.title: Can You Fix Your Thyroid with a Diet Change?
signals.summary: Harrison answers an audience question about whether thyroid conditions require cutting gluten, dairy, nightshades, coffee, and other supposedly 'inflammatory' foods, walking through why the evidence doesn't support elimination diets for thyroid health — a case study in how 'dietary cure' framing colonizes endocrine conditions.

signals.title: Evidence as content
signals.summary: Horning argues AI-generated 'news' clips, from fake Iran war footage to fake traffic-camera crashes, are parasitical on the tropes of evidence: the documentary look becomes a formal genre quality that mimics verifiability while inviting viewers to disavow any need for verification. Nobody is really tricked; slop's dismissibility is its appeal, and its harm is eroding collective responsibility for shared information, with both AI fakes and nostalgic 'seeing is believing' empiricism reflecting the same reactionary wish for images to do our political thinking for us.

signals.title: Reading is magic
signals.summary: Expanding his Jacobin essay on post-literacy, Kriss uses Alexander Luria's 1931 experiments with illiterate Uzbek peasants to show how reading restructures cognition toward abstraction, then argues collapsing literacy (Bleak House-baffled English majors, streamers as oral-culture bards) is returning us to a 'second peasanthood.' Against liberal panic he notes literacy itself bred mystic manias and nationalism; the post-literate future will be grounded in direct sensory experience again, except nothing we see, an AI-generated image world, will be real.

signals.title: If you let AI do your writing, I will come to your house and kill you
signals.summary: A comic-furious polemic arguing AI prose is structurally detectable because LLMs are 'permanently hallucinating', producing portentous filler ('we don't just serve food, we serve moments') whether writing catering websites or prize-winning fiction. Kriss catalogues AI-written Commonwealth Prize stories, NYT Modern Love columns, TV dialogue, and MPs' op-eds, concluding the only inviolably human literary forms left are those driven by lust, rage, and grievance, hence the titular death threat.

signals.title: A fire was in my head
signals.summary: A travelogue of a family gathering in County Antrim that becomes a meditation on likeable and unlikeable peoples: Kriss contrasts the globally beloved Irish with Ulster Loyalists, 'an entire people living on the wrong side of history,' and slyly maps his own Jewish self-consciousness (opening with a trip to occupied Hebron) onto the luckless, unloveable Prod.

signals.title: how to get really good at picking up your dog (or child)
signals.summary: Link Letter 198 arguing that the real reason to train is carrying the beings you love — strength as caregiving capacity rather than aesthetics — plus a sharp item on why the manosphere has embraced 'Pilates girls' as a feminine-fitness ideal.

signals.title: why can't anyone stop talking about protein?
signals.summary: Link Letter 201 on protein discourse saturation — '[massages temples] it won't stop' — with Johnston, who helped popularize eating more protein for lifters, reckoning with how the macro became an inescapable marketing layer across food culture; she promises to 'take her lumps' for her own role.

signals.title: the art of bending down
signals.summary: Link Letter 203 reframing childcare as 'primal movement' — the endless bending, squatting, and floor transitions of caring for small children as legitimate functional training — alongside items on an ACL-recovery documentary and the low-testosterone panic in men.

signals.title: a defense of doing nothing
signals.summary: A long essay arguing that 'the hardest thing some of us may do these days is sit at rest, in quiet contemplation' — rest as a trained capacity that optimization culture has eroded, from the writer whose whole project is effortful strength.

signals.title: go the frick outside
signals.summary: Link Letter 204 on why it's so hard to be ordinary in fitness culture, with Johnston's case for the 'super walk' — unglamorous, unquantified outdoor movement as the antidote to performance-tracked exercise.

signals.title: Insurance barely covers PT, but covers so much acupuncture and chiropractic; why?
signals.summary: An investigation into the political economy of American rehab care: why insurance plans ration evidence-based physical therapy to a handful of visits while generously covering acupuncture and chiropractic — a structural answer to why bodies get alternative medicine instead of strength-based recovery.

signals.title: having it all is not the same as doing it all
signals.summary: An Ask A Swole Woman response to 'can I nurse a baby and get jacked at the same time?': Johnston separates having a full life from performing every ambition simultaneously, applying her anti-optimization ethic to postpartum training, energy budgets, and the pressure on new mothers to recomposition their bodies on a deadline.

signals.title: hear me out: it's okay to date your fellow gym members
signals.summary: Johnston defends the gym as a genuine third space against the loneliness epidemic — including, with rules, as a place to date — pushing back on the etiquette consensus that romantic attention at the gym is inherently predatory; plus notes on training to actual failure and 'making a deadlift from scratch.'

signals.title: Milan in Review, Pt I: Salone's big hype problem, plus Monica's top picks
signals.summary: Jill Singer argues Salone del Mobile 2026 reached its 'terminal hype' phase: two-hour VIP queues, fashion-house activations (and a McDonald's ball pit), celebrity takes, and the fetishization of never-seen palazzos and a Portaluppi bomb shelter made access the week's only currency. She calls it the weakest, least innovative edition in memory and asks whether brands could invest their marketing budgets in designers themselves instead.

signals.title: Milan in Review, Part II: Jill's Top Picks
signals.summary: Second installment of Sight Unseen's three-part critical Salone report: Jill Singer's favorite presentations from the fair, pointedly noting that the editors found only one product under $200 all week — a data point in the newsletter's running argument about Milan's affordability and exclusivity problem.

signals.title: Milan in Review, Part III: Our Top 5 Exhibitions
signals.summary: Closing installment of the Milan report, ranking the five exhibitions that justified the trip despite the fair's hype problem — including a London duo at the top of their craft game and an antiques-filled apartment show, reflecting this Salone's turn toward historical interiors as exhibition settings.

signals.title: Murano glass, plaster flowers, mosaic tables: All the hits from New York Design Month so far
signals.summary: Mid-NYCxDesign editorial dispatch tracking the strongest launches of New York Design Month — In Common With's Murano glass Cosmos chandelier among them — and floating a trend thesis for the season: whether 2026 is 'the year of the woman welder,' as metalwork by women dominates the emerging-designer field.

signals.title: The Best of New York Design Week, From Nightlights to Fish Tables
signals.summary: Sight Unseen's wrap-up of New York Design Week 2026, surveying the standout objects — from nightlights to fish tables — and highlighting the Devin Wilde and Astraeus Clarke collaboration as the week's dream-team pairing.

signals.title: Ceramic 'burlwood,' vintage nightclub chairs, bronze reliefs, and more from Lisbon Design Week
signals.summary: Report from Lisbon Design Week framed as 'proof that small design fairs are thriving in 2026' — an implicit counterpoint to the editors' earlier Salone critique — spotlighting ceramic faux-burlwood, vintage nightclub chairs, and bronze reliefs from Portugal's smaller-scale, designer-centered fair circuit.

signals.title: An Indie Drama About Leaving China Finds an Audience at Home
signals.summary: An independent drama about emigration — the 'runxue' impulse to leave China — has unexpectedly resonated with domestic audiences, suggesting that stories of departure now function as a mirror for viewers negotiating their own ambivalence about staying.

signals.title: 'Unbelievably Accurate': The Niche Dating Apps Sweeping China's Colleges
signals.summary: Feature on niche matchmaking apps spreading through Chinese universities, where students praise the uncanny accuracy of their matches — a signal that young Chinese are abandoning mass dating platforms for smaller, identity-sorted services that promise compatibility over volume.

signals.title: Handmade: Two Chinese Productions Go Viral for Skipping AI
signals.summary: Two Chinese productions won viral acclaim precisely for not using AI, making demonstrative handcraft a marketable aesthetic value. Captures an emerging counter-current in Chinese media consumption where human labor itself becomes the selling point amid AI saturation.

signals.title: Before WeChat, There Were Qiaopi Writers
signals.summary: Portrait of 77-year-old Jiang Mingdian, possibly the last working qiaopi letter-writer, whose trade once connected Chinese families with relatives abroad through remittance letters. A human-angle meditation on communication, diaspora kinship, and what instant messaging displaced.

signals.title: Flying Solo: The Rise of China's One-Person Companies
signals.summary: Feature on a new form of solo entrepreneurship taking root in China as AI tools let individuals perform work that once required whole teams — a reconfiguration of career identity in which the one-person company becomes both an economic hedge and a lifestyle statement amid a tight job market.

signals.title: The Rage, Love, and Loneliness Behind China's Toxic Sports Fandom
signals.summary: A feature on how celebrity-fandom logics — shippers, solo stans, data spreadsheets — have engulfed elite Chinese table tennis, generating online attacks severe enough that authorities have stepped in. Reads the toxicity as displaced love and loneliness, showing fan-circle culture jumping from entertainment into state-prized sport.

signals.title: What China's 'Drama Girls' Really Want
signals.summary: Scholar Wu Xiaoyan argues that the young women powering China's musical-theater boom — often dismissed as irrational 'drama girls' — are enacting deeper generational changes in how meaning, intimacy, and escape are sought, with repeat ticket-buying and performer fandom functioning as emotional infrastructure rather than mere consumption.

signals.title: How Emojis Have Become a Language Within a Language in China
signals.summary: Liu Yuli traces how pinyin input quirks, homophonic wordplay, the 'abstract' (chouxiang) subculture, and platform keyword-censorship evasion turned emojis into a phonetic code on the Chinese internet — pill emoji for 'impending doom', peach for Taobao, shark for 'kill'. The paradox: the more universal emojis become, the more culturally tribal their meanings grow, building a new Tower of Babel between generations and in-groups.

signals.title: Shitmaxxing and $300M Bagels
signals.summary: On 'shitmaxxing' — the fiber-and-gut-health optimization discourse that has turned digestion into a maxxing vertical — paired with commentary on a $300M bagel chain valuation, as wellness culture and food-business froth converge on the same absurdist register.

signals.title: The Children Yearn for SNAX
signals.summary: Trend digest on convenience formats colonizing the fresh perimeter — shelf-stable hummus, frozen pasta sauce, and 'protein schmear' — read as evidence of younger consumers wanting snackified, functional versions of pantry basics.

signals.title: Does CPG Need A Deuxmoi?
signals.summary: Prompted by another 'Forbes 30 under 30 to jail pipeline' founder scandal, Hernández asks whether the food and beverage industry needs an anonymous gossip-accountability channel, since trade press and investor incentives keep founder misbehavior unreported until collapse.

signals.title: Bible Approved Protein Bar
signals.summary: Faith enters the functional-food chat: a 'Bible approved' protein bar alongside colostrum soda, electrolyte lollipops, and creatine donuts — evidence that religious framing is becoming another trust-signal layer in wellness CPG, and that performance ingredients are colonizing every indulgence format.

signals.title: Venture with a Side of Fries
signals.summary: A skeptical look at venture capital's renewed appetite for food: vitamin sprinkles as investable 'innovation' and the rise of AI-powered 'intelligent grocers,' continuing Snaxshot's running argument that funding flows to optimization gimmicks rather than food people actually want.

signals.title: Tinned Fish for Men
signals.summary: On the gendering of pantry staples: tinned fish gets a masculinity-coded rebrand while creatine migrates into cookies and a 'Korean Erewhon' emerges, all against a backdrop of escalating food fear-mongering used as a sales tactic in wellness CPG.

signals.title: STATE OF BEVERAGE
signals.summary: Snaxshot's flagship annual beverage industry report, opening with the observation that much of her 2023 state-of-beverage diagnosis still rings true — a claim that functional, hydration, and energy categories have consolidated around the same consumer anxieties rather than producing genuinely new demand.

signals.title: Tom Brady Wants You to Swallow His Good Nut
signals.summary: Hernández reads Tom Brady's innuendo-branded GoPuff coconut water 'Good Nut' as celebrity CPG finally learning to not take itself seriously, then maps post-Covid 'air hunger' commerce (Climatic Health's $95 supplement-loaded breathing device sold out in two weeks), cowboy cosplay spreading from Italian spaghetti-western beans to Aussie 'Texan' ranch, and matcha-infused olive oil as the 'pretty pantry paradigm.'

signals.title: 50 Ways to Meet Your Maker
signals.summary: Eddie Lakin shadows Dave Odd, Chicago's premier restaurant forager, hunting 'incredible (and free) edibles' in the suburbs — a look at the foraging supply chain feeding high-end menus and the risk calculus (the title's joke) of wild food.

signals.title: Cheers to the Publican!
signals.summary: An anniversary appraisal of Chicago's Publican — 'turns out you can indeed live a very long time on a diet of oysters, beer, and pork' — that reads the restaurant's longevity as a counter-case in an industry where institutions rarely survive two decades.

signals.title: Behind the Curtain
signals.summary: Lisa Shames profiles a celebrated Chicago chef returning with an interactive multimedia dinner, anchored by his quote that 'stability, a 401K, insurance, and being underworked' weren't enough — a diagnostic snapshot of post-fine-dining career economics, where chefs trade security for creative spectacle formats.

signals.title: 99 Problems and A Boka Ain't One
signals.summary: Framed by the line 'the greatest trick the devil ever pulled was convincing us via YouTube that we could fix anything,' Nagrant uses DIY-culture overconfidence as a lens on Boka's enduring excellence — an essay about competence, expertise, and why some things should be left to professionals.

signals.title: The Secrets
signals.summary: Nagrant plays out the conceit of a secret critic society whose 'sacred texts' pass from Grimod de La Reynière through Craig Claiborne, Ruth Reichl, and Gael Greene, then adds his own rule #1273: investment in branding is directly related to restaurant quality — 'the more your restaurant logo looks like a Stan Lee comic imagined by AI, the more likely your restaurant sucks.' Hung on a strip-mall tempura review.

signals.title: Sometimes You Need a "W"
signals.summary: A personal essay on mortality and family conflict and the way eating consoles: 50-year-old red wine, hot dogs, Portuguese food, and baseball assembled as the small wins that get you through. Food criticism as memoir rather than verdict.

signals.title: The Peptide Boom is Coming for South Asians
signals.summary: Tulika Bose investigates the marketing of injectable peptide 'Wolverine' and 'glow' stacks to South Asians as fixes for the metabolic and skin issues the community has long struggled with — a wellness-optimization trend that targets ethnic-specific insecurities while carrying poorly understood health risks.

signals.title: They Left Socialism. Their Children Are Selling It Back.
signals.summary: Tulika Bose explores the generational rift in how South Asians understand socialism: immigrant parents who fled the scarcity of License Raj-era India and Left-ruled Kolkata bristle as their American-born children embrace democratic socialism — showing that 'socialism' means entirely different things depending on who you ask and what they lived through.

signals.title: Shola Was the Met Gala's Most Unexpected Star
signals.summary: Snigdha Sur gets an exclusive look at how designer Mayyur Girotra and Diya Mehta Jatia brought shola — a dying Bengali craft of carving featherweight milky-white sponge-wood, traditionally used for idol ornaments — to the Met Gala via Kolkata artisans, putting an endangered vernacular craft on fashion's most-watched stage.

signals.title: When Did South Asian Weddings Become 'Content'?
signals.summary: Aadvika Gupta reports on couples paying premium fees for phone-first 'wedding content creators' who produce trending reels and TikToks alongside traditional photographers — the multi-day South Asian wedding, already a theater of status, is being re-choreographed for the algorithm, with virality now a line item in the wedding budget.

signals.title: Will the Wasians Let Us Sit With Them?
signals.summary: Tulika Bose dissects the viral 'Wasian meetup' that drew thousands to Central Park's Sheep Meadow — complete with celebrity-lookalike contests — and the backlash from South Asian and other mixed-Asian attendees told they didn't count because 'Wasian' implies East Asian. The episode exposed a new colorist hierarchy over who gets to claim mixed-Asian identity, with whiteness still at its center.

signals.title: The Ranveer Singh Ban is About More Than One Star
signals.summary: Ishita Sengupta reads the Federation of Western India Cine Employees' unprecedented industry-wide ban on Ranveer Singh — reportedly stemming from his fallout with Farhan Akhtar over the stalled 'Don 3' — as a symptom of a new Bollywood hierarchy, in which unions, producers, and a post-pandemic star system are renegotiating who actually holds power over even A-list actors.

signals.title: Before Seersucker Was Southern, It Was Indian
signals.summary: Nikash Harapanahalli traces how seersucker — a puckered cotton fabric from India (from the Persian 'shir o shakar') — traveled through colonial trade to become the genteel summer uniform of the American South, a case study in how colonial-era Indian textiles get absorbed and rebranded as Western heritage aesthetics.

signals.title: Yes, You Can Be Muslim and Queer
signals.summary: After a news outlet branded Zohran Mamdani and Sadiq Khan 'fake' Muslims for celebrating Pride Month, Tulika Bose talks to queer Muslims who reject the premise that their faith and sexuality are incompatible — a pushback against gatekeeping of Muslim identity from both Islamophobes and conservative co-religionists.

signals.title: How Much of Substack Is Actually AI?
signals.summary: Lorenz ran thousands of posts from Substack's top bestselling newsletters through AI detector Pangram and found some of the platform's biggest 'writers' aren't writing their own work — a data-driven look at how AI-generated text has quietly colonized a platform marketed on authentic human voice.

signals.title: A pro-AI dark money group tried to recruit me
signals.summary: First-person investigation into the pro-AI influence machine: Lorenz recounts being approached by email to participate in a dark-money-funded pro-AI advocacy effort, using the recruitment attempt to expose how AI industry money is quietly enlisting journalists and creators to shape public sentiment.

signals.title: The Influencer Industrial Complex is Warping Local Politics
signals.summary: Reporting on how political content creators are building their personal brands by 'collabbing' with local candidates, often without proper disclosure — extending influencer marketing dynamics into local elections where small audiences and thin media coverage make undisclosed creator endorsements especially distorting.

signals.title: No, Creators Don't 'Deserve to Be Paid' for This
signals.summary: An argument against the booming influencer political advertising industry: Lorenz contends that undisclosed paid political content from creators is poisoning democracy, and rejects the creator-economy framing that influencers 'deserve to be paid' for political speech that audiences receive as authentic opinion.

signals.title: The Bounty Economy Is Breaking Reality
signals.summary: Lorenz names a new phase of the attention economy — the 'bounty economy' — after Pump.fun launched Pump Fun GO, a pay-anyone-to-do-anything bounty platform where users get paid to post election fraud conspiracies and debase themselves for small sums. Together with Polymarket, Kalshi, and 'UGC marketing,' she argues these platforms are building a synthetic reality where what we encounter online and IRL is increasingly commissioned performance.

signals.title: Yes, You Belong In The Gym
signals.summary: The opening of Sole-Smith's gym arc: she tells readers fat people belong in fitness spaces while admitting she herself hasn't joined one — an honest accounting of how anticipated fatphobia, not lack of motivation, keeps larger bodies out of gyms.

signals.title: If Protein Bros Can Pose For Photos
signals.summary: If gym bros can unselfconsciously document their bodies mid-flex, fat people deserve the same permission to be photographed: an argument about visibility, who is allowed to take up space in images, and the double standard in body documentation culture.

signals.title: How I'm Getting 8+ Hours of Sleep a Night
signals.summary: With the pointed subtitle 'the answer is not protein shots,' Sole-Smith describes actually sleeping well through behavioral and life changes rather than the supplement-and-optimization products wellness culture sells for sleep — a quiet counter to sleepmaxxing commerce.

signals.title: Get The Fun Glasses.
signals.summary: An advice-column essay against deferred living: get the fun glasses now rather than waiting for a thinner, 'better' future body — Sole-Smith's anti-diet framework applied to everyday consumer decisions where fat people are taught to postpone pleasure.

signals.title: Fine, We Talked About Peptides
signals.summary: A reluctant engagement with peptide discourse — the next-wave injectable wellness trend riding GLP-1 momentum — examining how 'peptides' have become diet culture's new euphemism layer; bundled with notes on spring dinner parties and the body politics of the mirror selfie.

signals.title: In My Gym Girl Era?
signals.summary: Sole-Smith reports from the end of her newsletter arc about joining a gym as a fat woman, weighing what a 'gym girl era' means when fitness culture assumes weight loss as the goal; plus a reader debate on who gets to claim the 'single mom' label.

signals.title: AI's Economics Don't Make Sense
signals.summary: An argument that the basic unit economics of generative AI are broken: flat monthly subscriptions can't price users whose LLM costs vary wildly, and AI data centers are built for perfection — requiring near-100% utilization with at best ~70% margins and six years of depreciation to break even — while serving a customer base of unprofitable startups, meaning prices must eventually rise dramatically.

signals.title: Am I Meant To Be Impressed?
signals.summary: Zitron dissects the circular AI economy: OpenAI and Anthropic expected industries to grow around their tech, but the only way to create demand was to fund it themselves. He weighs Microsoft's $37 billion AI revenue run rate and Amazon's $15 billion against their costs, comparing the industry to perpetual-motion enthusiasts who have actually failed catastrophically.

signals.title: Where Are All The Data Centers?
signals.summary: An investigation into the gap between announced AI compute capacity and reality: the supposed gigawatts of 'incredible, unstoppable demand' aren't translating into revenue, Zitron argues, likely because much of the capacity doesn't exist — tech companies underestimated how hard physical data center construction is, and money can't compress its limits.

signals.title: AI Is Too Expensive
signals.summary: Zitron tallies the full cost stack of AI data centers — electricity, staffing, taxes, insurance — atop $800+ billion of hyperscaler capex over three years, with another $700 billion planned for 2026 and $1 trillion for 2027, concluding the industry needs $3 trillion in AI-specific revenue just to break even and $6 trillion for the buildout to be anything but a wash.

signals.title: Anthropic's "Profitability" Swindle
signals.summary: A pointed rebuttal to the Wall Street Journal's story that Anthropic is 'about to have its first profitable quarter,' arguing the claim rests on accounting framing that excludes the actual costs of training and running models, and that uncritical business press is laundering AI-lab narratives.

signals.title: Revenge of The Business Idiot
signals.summary: A sequel to 'The Era of the Business Idiot' arguing that LLMs primarily impress professionals who don't want to do their jobs, and that white-collar work is enslaved to a middle-management layer that never understood the work it supervises. He reads Mustafa Suleyman's claim that all white-collar labor will be automated in 18 months as compensation for unimpressive products.

signals.title: AI Doesn't Have ROI
signals.summary: Zitron's answer to why nobody can show return on investment from enterprise AI: there isn't one. LLMs speed up some tasks, but the value and accuracy of that speedup degrades as task complexity rises, making 'AI ROI' a category error rather than a measurement problem.

signals.title: AI Is Slowing Down
signals.summary: Zitron argues the AI buildout's math has stopped working: OpenAI and Anthropic project roughly $60 billion in combined 2026 revenue against infrastructure commitments that require on the order of $400 billion a year, with OpenAI alone expecting $50 billion in 2026 compute spend. The shift to token-based billing in Q1 2026, he argues, exposed stalling demand and growth.

signals.title: The Celebration of Suffering Edition
signals.summary: On Ozempic, cynicism, and 'good tech': why culture valorizes visible suffering and effort, and why frictionless technological fixes provoke distrust even when they work.

signals.title: The Golf Umbrella Edition
signals.summary: A case for the golf umbrella as an affordable luxury, drawing on caddie culture and the rules around 'casual water' to argue that oversized, purpose-built objects deliver outsized everyday pleasure.

signals.title: The Performative Fitness Edition
signals.summary: On Strava, streak tracking, and the validation trap: how social fitness platforms have turned exercise into an audience-facing performance, and what is lost when working out becomes content.

signals.title: The World Cup Squad Edition
signals.summary: On how diaspora communities and dual-national players are reshaping World Cup squad construction, producing new types of tournament teams and complicating what a national side represents.

signals.title: The AI Mirror Edition
signals.summary: Noah Brier argues that AI functions as a mirror rather than a corrupting force: panics over AI in education and accountability mostly expose failures that predate the technology — the question is 'where we went wrong first.'

signals.title: The Enantiodromia Edition
signals.summary: Applies Carl Jung's concept of enantiodromia — the tendency of things to flip into their opposite — to digital culture, arguing that algorithmic feed saturation is reversing into a desire for high-context environments and predicting 'purer feeds ahead.'

signals.title: The Ugly, Essential Books Edition
signals.summary: An essay on misguided first editions, sentimentality, and house moves — why the ugly, unloved-looking books on our shelves are often the essential ones, and what owning physical books for emotional rather than aesthetic reasons says about objects and attachment.

signals.title: The Real McCoy's Edition
signals.summary: Colin Nagy on the Japanese brand The Real McCoy's and reproduction Americana: how obsessive fidelity to vintage American military and workwear garments has matured from faithful copying into a design language of its own — 'moving beyond reproduction.'
